title: Mastering 4th Nerve Palsy: The Trochlear Checklist
summary: The Superior Oblique (SO) muscle is a unique ocular motor player. This guide provides a deep dive into the anatomy, diagnosis, and management of CN IV palsy, distinguishing between congenital, acquired, unilateral, and bilateral presentations.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy results in dysfunction of the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle, leading to a characteristic vertical, torsional, and often horizontal diplopia. It is the most common cause of acquired vertical diplopia in clinical practice. The CN IV is unique: it is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally from the brainstem, it has the longest intracranial course (75mm), and it is the only one where all fibers decussate before exiting.

sections.title: The Decisive Differentiation: Congenital vs. Acquired

rows: Normal head posture in the past
SO tendon may be lax, redundant, or absent

sections.title: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is Hypertropic in primary position.
Step 2: Determine if the Hypertropia increases in Left or Right gaze.
Step 3: Determine if the Hypertropia increases on Right or Left head tilt.

sections.title: When to Suspect Bilateral Palsy
content: Traumatic etiology (especially severe head injury)
Reversing Hypertropia: RHT on R-tilt, LHT on L-tilt
Excyclotorsion > 10-15 degrees (Double Maddox Rod)
V-pattern esotropia (>15PD difference between up/down gaze)
Chin down posture with bilateral SO underaction

sections.title: Primary Actions of the Superior Oblique
Clinical Presentation & Symptoms
content: Vertical diplopia (worse on downgaze/reading)
Torsional diplopia (objects appear tilted)
Compensatory head tilt (away from the side of the lesion)
Facial asymmetry (in long-standing congenital cases)
Asthenopia and neck pain from chronic tilt

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Sensorimotor Exam: Cover test, 3-step test, and versions/ductions.
2. Torsion Assessment: Double Maddox Rod or Fundus Photography (looking for macular depression).
3. Fusional Amplitudes: Using a Prism Bar to check vertical ranges.
4. Physical Exam: Check for FAT (Facial Asymmetry) and old family photos.
5. Neurological Exam: Check other CNs (III, VI) and look for long-tract signs.
6. Imaging: MRI Brain/Orbits if non-traumatic/non-ischemic or if multiple CN involvements.

content.explanation: Symmetric (often), Skew (rule out), Small (hypertropia in primary), Significant (torsion >10°).

sections.title: Management Strategy: Non-Surgical
content: Observation: Especially for ischemic cases (6-9 months for recovery).
Prism Therapy: Fresnel prisms for temporary relief; ground-in prisms for stable deviations (<10PD).
Occlusion: Patching one eye to eliminate diplopia during the recovery phase.
Botulinum Toxin: Injection into the Inferior Oblique (IO) to reduce overaction (less common).

rows: Side of gaze opposite the palsy
Side of gaze toward the palsy

sections.title: Surgical Landmarks: Harada-Ito
content: 1. Identify the SO tendon via a superotemporal peritomy.
2. Split the anterior 1/3 of the SO tendon fibers.
3. Transpose these anterior fibers anteriorly and laterally (near the LR).
4. This selectively enhances intorsion without affecting vertical balance.

sections.title: Red Flags: When it's not a simple IV
content: Associated Ptosis or Pupil Involvement (Check CN III)
Contralateral Hemiparesis (Brainstem lesion/Weber-like)
Papilledema (Increased Intracranial Pressure)
Variable Deviation or Cogan's Twitch (Myasthenia Gravis)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: If a patient tilts their head to the RIGHT to fix a LHT, they have a LEFT CN IV palsy.
SO underaction on versions often leads to compensatory Inferior Oblique overaction (IOOA).
In trauma, the CN IV is vulnerable because the long nerves cross over the tentorial edge.
Subjective torsion is often less than objective torsion in congenital cases due to cortical adaptation.
The 'Maddox Rod' is the gold standard for quantifying torsion in the clinic.
